lines: Morgan Kim
+1 (555) 010-8173 | morgan.kim@example.com | example.com/code/mkim
EDUCATION
Clearwater Institute of Technology | B.S. in Electrical Engineering | Metro City, USA | Sep 2017 - May 2021
EXPERIENCE
Voltline Robotics | Embedded Software Engineer | Metro City, USA | Mar 2023 - Jun 2025
- Improved update speed by 60% by compressing firmware images and resuming interrupted downloads.
- Wrote a hardware-in-the-loop test rig that ran 400 motor-control tests on every firmware build.
- Added a crash logger that saved the last 2 seconds of sensor data to flash, which found the root cause of 5 field failures.
- Sampled the motor's 5 kHz vibration signal at 8 kHz so the fault detector could capture it without aliasing.
- Fixed a race condition on the counter shared by the interrupt handler and the main loop by declaring the counter volatile.
- Rewrote the motor-controller firmware for a warehouse robot fleet of 300 units, cutting control-loop jitter from 120 to 15 microseconds and field motor faults by 60%.
Clearwater Sensors | Hardware Test Engineer | Metro City, USA | Apr 2022 - Feb 2023
- Automated end-of-line tests for a humidity sensor, cutting test time per unit from 90 to 25 seconds across 20,000 units a month.
- Traced a batch of early field failures to a solder-paste change; the findings updated the reflow profile and cut returns from 2.1% to 0.4%.
- Wrote the calibration procedure for the sensor line, cutting calibration drift complaints from 15 to 2 a quarter.
- Designed a test fixture that checked 8 boards at once, raising station throughput from 40 to 150 boards an hour.
PROJECTS
Low-Power Weather Station | Independent Project | C, STM32 | Jan 2025 - Present
- Engineered a next-generation, innovation-driven IoT solution that redefines sustainable environmental sensing.
- Cut average current from 4.2 mA to 0.9 mA by sleeping between readings and batching radio transmissions.
- Published the schematics and firmware openly, and a local school built two stations from them.
Formula Student Electric Car | Electronics Lead, Team of 12 | C | Sep 2019 - May 2021
- Worked on firmware and testing for the robot fleet's motor controllers.
- The CAN-bus firmware for the dashboard was written and tested against the motor controller before each race.
- Rewrote motor-control firmware for a fleet of about 300 robots, cutting control-loop jitter eightfold and motor faults by more than half.
SKILLS
Tools: C, C++, STM32, oscilloscopes, FPGA
Methods: firmware, hardware-in-the-loop testing, CAN, low-power design

items.says: The timeline leaves 10 months unexplained between the degree and the first listed professional role.
items.because: The degree ends in May 2021, while the first role begins in April 2022.

items.says: The section order should put experience first, followed by projects, education, and skills.
items.because: More than three years of relevant professional work should establish the candidate’s direction first.

items.says: “Update speed” does not identify the measure behind the 60% improvement.
items.because: The reader cannot tell whether update duration fell or transfer throughput increased.

items.says: The 60% improvement lacks a starting time or throughput for comparison.
items.because: Without a baseline, the percentage is difficult to judge or defend.

items.says: The test-rig bullet gives testing volume but no result from running the tests.
items.because: Four hundred tests does not show whether the rig caught regressions or improved validation.

items.says: The crash logger is credited with finding the root causes instead of the engineers who used its data.
items.because: “Which found” assigns the investigative result to a tool and weakens ownership of the work.

items.says: Sampling a 5 kHz signal at 8 kHz cannot capture it without aliasing.
items.because: The rate must exceed 10 kHz, with suitable anti-alias filtering, to capture that component without aliasing.

items.says: The sampling bullet gives no resulting fault-detection outcome.
items.because: The reader cannot tell whether detection improved or a previously missed fault became detectable.

items.says: Declaring the shared counter volatile did not fix the race condition.
items.because: Volatile provides neither atomicity nor synchronization between the interrupt handler and main loop.

items.says: The race-condition bullet does not say what symptom or result changed afterward.
items.because: The implementation detail alone does not show whether corrupted counts, crashes, or another failure were prevented.

items.says: The firmware rewrite does not identify the embedded technique behind the improvements.
items.because: A technical hiring manager cannot see what firmware expertise produced the results.

items.says: The 60% reduction does not specify whether it concerns motor-fault counts or rates.
The strongest achievement should open the Voltline entry.
“A batch of early field failures” is awkward and delays the direct object of “traced.”
The calibration bullet does not show the technical work behind the procedure.
items.because: A hardware-test reader cannot tell what calibration skill the candidate applied.

items.says: “15 to 2 a quarter” makes the measurement period less immediately readable.
The weather-station opening is promotional filler rather than a concrete description of the work.
items.because: Its promotional phrases do not tell the reader what the station measured, enabled, or improved.

items.says: The bullet gives no concrete outcome or checkable evidence for its claims.
items.because: It provides no measurement or other checkable evidence.

items.says: The bullet does not identify a technical contribution or show how C or STM32 was applied.
The strongest weather-station result should open the project entry.
The current reduction lacks measurement conditions or a duty cycle.
items.because: Average current depends on how often the station sensed, woke, and transmitted.

items.says: The school-replication bullet does not say how the two stations were used or what they enabled.
items.because: Its impact stops at replication rather than showing practical use.

items.says: The publication wording is indirect and makes “them” ambiguous.
The bullet misattributes robot-fleet work to the Formula Student car project.
items.because: A Formula Student project concerns an electric race car, not a robot fleet.

items.says: “Worked on firmware and testing” is vague about the candidate’s contribution.
items.because: It gives no deliverable, result, or specific technical action and makes the candidate sound like a bystander.

items.says: The dashboard-firmware bullet uses passive wording that hides who did the work.
items.because: “Was written and tested” does not identify the candidate’s action.

items.says: The bullet does not identify the CAN-bus behavior validated or what the firmware enabled.
items.because: Testing before each race gives cadence, not pass criteria or evidence that telemetry, command handling, or fault reporting worked.

items.says: The 300-robot achievement is misattributed to the Formula Student project and duplicated under Voltline.
items.because: A single electric-car project does not fit a 300-robot deployment, and the same figures appear under Voltline.

items.says: The relative improvements do not define the jitter and motor-fault measures or their comparisons.
items.because: The reader cannot tell what counted as jitter or a motor fault.

items.says: The rewrite does not show the technical change behind the reported improvements.
items.because: The reader cannot see whether the work involved scheduling, timing, interrupts, control logic, or fault handling.

items.says: This bullet should not open the Formula Student entry.
The entries do not support the listed C++ and FPGA skills.
items.because: The experience and project descriptions show C and STM32 work but no C++ or FPGA task.
